source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically: problem solving, metacognition and sense-making (chapter)
finding: Through the 1970s there was little evidence that taught heuristics helped. Taught heuristics did not transfer to new domains (Wilson 1967, Smith 1973). Heuristic use correlated with performance only weakly (Kantowski, Kilpatrick, Lucas). Harvey and Romberg 1980: strategy teaching was promising but had not panned out.
numbers: No pooled effect size given. Correlations described only as relatively small.
quote: there was little empirical evidence to back up the sense that heuristics could be used as vehicles to enhanced problem solving
limits: Narrative review by an interested party. Older studies, mostly unpublished dissertations.
agent_relevance: A plain list of Polya heuristics in a prompt has a weak prior. Do not assume a menu helps without a measurement.

source: Begle (1979) as quoted in Schoenfeld (1992)
finding: Begle judged that strategies are both problem-specific and student-specific, so finding one or few strategies to teach all students is too simplistic.
numbers: none
quote: problem solving strategies are both problem- and student-specific often enough to suggest that finding one (or few) strategies ... are far too simplistic
limits: A 1979 opinion, read second-hand in Schoenfeld 1992. Later work (b03) partly answered it.
agent_relevance: Supports operator preconditions: a heuristic must be tied to problem features, not applied by default.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) discussion of Polya's strategies as descriptive not prescriptive
finding: Polya's strategies let you recognise a strategy in use but do not say how to carry it out. Special cases split into at least three different strategies for three problem classes: n=1,2,3 for integer-parameter series, easy-to-factor polynomials for root problems, initial values 0 and 1 for recursions. Trying the wrong special cases (n=1,2,3 on the polynomial problem) gives a wild goose chase.
numbers: Three worked problems; one coarse heuristic split into three precise ones. Claim: a dozen more could be found.
quote: the characterizations of them were descriptive rather than prescriptive
limits: Worked examples, not an experiment. Claim that students can learn the fine-grained versions cites Schoenfeld 1985a, not re-checked here.
agent_relevance: Core design point for operators: each needs a precondition (what problem feature triggers it) and a concrete procedure. Name the sub-variant, not the Polya label.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) teaching heuristics as drilled algorithms
finding: Textbooks show a strategy, give practice on it, then test it. Schoenfeld says taught that way a strategy becomes an algorithm and no longer a heuristic. Teaching real problem solving is harder for the teacher: they must judge whether a student approach is fruitful and when to intervene.
numbers: none
quote: they are no longer heuristics in Polya's sense; they are mere algorithms
limits: Qualitative argument from classroom observation.
agent_relevance: Drilling one heuristic per problem type in a prompt may buy accuracy on that type but not the open-ended skill. Measure on unseen problem types.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) control study: novice solution attempts before and after a problem-solving course
finding: In a collection of over 100 videotapes of college and high school students on unfamiliar problems, about 60 percent of attempts were read, pick a direction fast, and pursue it regardless. After a course in which the instructor kept asking What are you doing, why, how does it help, fewer than 20 percent were of that type, with a reported rise in success.
numbers: About 60 percent before, under 20 percent after. No N, no test statistic, no control group given in this chapter. The better part of a semester was needed.
quote: roughly sixty percent of the solution attempts are of the read, make a decision quickly, and pursue that direction come hell or high water variety
limits: Summary of a lab course taught by the researcher. Success increase is stated, not quantified here. Likely demand effects.
agent_relevance: The failure is lack of control, not lack of heuristics. Supports the schema rule: monitor and abandon on a signal, G1. A scaffold can impose the three questions cheaply; humans needed months.

source: Lester, Garofalo and Kroll (1989) seventh-grade metacognition instruction, as summarised in Schoenfeld (1992)
finding: Teacher served as external monitor before, during and after problem solving (ten teaching actions, including relate to earlier problems and name strategies). Instruction covered guess-and-check, working backwards and looking for patterns. Authors concluded metacognitive growth needs sustained exposure over a long period, is best when organised by the teacher, and is hard to keep up when students struggle with basics.
numbers: 16.1 hours over 12 weeks, 35.7 percent of class time; two classes (one regular, one advanced). No effect sizes in the summary.
limits: Two classes. Quantitative outcomes not given in the chapter, only conclusions.
agent_relevance: Human heuristic training works through an external monitor that prompts at fixed points. The program in our schema plays that monitor role.

source: Bruun (2013) Elementary teachers' perspectives of mathematics problem solving strategies, quoting Hembree (1992) meta-analysis
finding: Second-hand report of Hembree 1992 (487 reports). Explicit training was essential: practice in the sub-skills without direct intervention did not improve performance. Checking work, diagrams and heuristics went with higher scores. Following step-by-step procedures did worse than flexible approaches. No benefit from rereading or restating the problem, or from pure trial and error. Largest clear effect from teachers specially trained in heuristics. Knowing how to drop extraneous data gave a large effect; guess-and-test and composing problems gave more modest effects.
numbers: 487 reports. The effect sizes are not given in this source; I could not open Hembree 1992 itself (JRME, paywalled).
quote: explicit training was found essential; without direct intervention and oversight, practice in using these sub skills did not result in better performance
limits: Second-hand. Hembree numbers unverified. Pooled studies mix heuristics, grades and outcome tests.
agent_relevance: Two hints for operators: diagram and representation operators have the best human support; restate-the-problem has none. Compare with b18 where elaboration helped some LLMs.

source: Trinchero and Sala (2016) Chess training and mathematical problem solving: the role of teaching heuristics in transfer of learning
finding: Cluster-controlled trial with a pre-test and post-test. Chess lessons taught by chess instructors, who taught chess problem-solving heuristics, raised maths problem-solving more than the same lessons by school teachers (no heuristics) or no lessons. Group was the only significant effect in the model; the school-teacher group did not beat control.
numbers: 931 pupils in grades 3-5, 53 classes, 20 schools: chess instructors 320 (18 classes), school teachers 220 (12), control 391 (23). About 14 to 15 hours of training. Maths gain 0.56 (adjusted 0.60, d 0.50) vs 0.23 (0.15, d 0.20) vs 0.15 (0.15, d 0.13).
limits: Not randomised at pupil level. The instructor and heuristics factors are confounded, since only the instructors taught heuristics. d is gain over pre-test SD, not a between-group effect. Authors note the chess-to-maths transfer literature is mostly negative.
agent_relevance: One of few trials where taught general heuristics transferred to another domain, medium effect (d 0.5). Mere exposure to practice did nothing, in line with b07.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting (ACL 2023)
finding: Asking a model to first devise a plan, then carry it out, beats zero-shot chain of thought on math. The PS+ version adds extract relevant variables, calculate intermediate results, and attend to calculation and commonsense. PS+ roughly matches 8-shot manual CoT on average.
numbers: text-davinci-003, six math sets, average accuracy: zero-shot CoT 70.4, PS 73.5, PS+ 76.7, manual 8-shot CoT 77.6. GSM8K: CoT 56.4, PS 57.0, PS+ 59.3. MultiArith 83.8, 92.2 (PS), 91.8 (PS+). SVAMP 69.9, 70.8, 75.7.
limits: Old model (GPT-3 family). GSM8K gain with plain PS is 0.6 points, i.e. noise-sized; most of the gain is on the easy sets and from PS+ details. Authors say the model is sensitive to prompt wording. Table columns were garbled by text extraction; row mapping checked against the paper text.
agent_relevance: The nearest measured version of Polya's plan stage. A plan step alone gives little on a hard set; the explicit variable and calculation cues carry the gain. Needs re-test on current models.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve error analysis on GSM8K
finding: Planning reduces missing-step errors somewhat but not semantic misunderstanding. Semantic errors stayed the largest class.
numbers: 100 wrong GSM8K answers. Zero-shot CoT: calculation 7 percent, missing step 12, semantic 27. PS: 7, 10, 26. PS+ row not re-read.
limits: One annotator pass on 100 items; error types are coarse.
agent_relevance: Understanding errors (the Polya understand-the-problem phase) are not fixed by a plan prompt. That points to operators for restating and checking the problem, with code checks.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: Decompose into easier subproblems and solve them in order (Polya auxiliary problem and decomposing). Huge gain on a compositional generalisation test, tiny gain on GSM8K overall, real gain only on long problems.
numbers: code-davinci-002. SCAN length split: CoT 16.2, least-to-most 99.7. GSM8K overall: CoT 60.87 vs 62.39; by steps: 2 steps 76.68 vs 74.53 (worse), 3 steps 67.29 vs 68.91, 4 steps 59.39 vs 59.73, 5+ steps 39.07 vs 45.23. DROP non-football 74.77 vs 82.45.
limits: Authors note that almost every GSM8K failure is solvable with a hand-made decomposition: the model's own decomposition is the weak part. Prompt tailored per dataset.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for the decompose operator: it hurts slightly on short problems (2 steps) and helps on long ones. Gate it on estimated problem length or a failed first attempt.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back: evoking reasoning via abstraction (ICLR 2024)
finding: First ask the model for the high-level principle behind the question, then answer. This is Polya's generalise. Helps most on physics and chemistry multiple choice and on time-sensitive QA; with GPT-4 the gain over plain CoT is small.
numbers: MMLU physics / chemistry. PaLM-2L: base 66.4 / 70.9, CoT 65 / 75.3, Step-Back 73.2 / 81.8. GPT-4: base 69.4 / 80.9, CoT 82.9 / 85.3, Step-Back 84.5 / 85.6 (gain over CoT 1.6 and 0.3, inside the stated spread). Llama2-70B: CoT 59.3 / 64.1, Step-Back 64.8 / 66.7. Abstract: TimeQA +27, MuSiQue +7.
limits: CoT on PaLM-2L did not help physics (65 vs 66.4). Not a math-competition set.
agent_relevance: Generalise helps a weaker model, but the margin shrinks with a stronger one. Use it as a second attempt, not a default, and check against held-out signals.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Model writes its own related problems and solutions (Polya: have you seen a related problem) before solving. Beats zero-shot CoT and fixed few-shot CoT on average, +4 points.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5-turbo: 5-shot CoT 75.0 vs self-generated exemplars 77.8 (table columns garbled by text extraction, so the row mapping is approximate). MATH about 33.0 vs 37.3 (GPT-3.5-turbo), about 27.1 vs 34.8 (PaLM-2). Average gain from the abstract: +4 percent.
limits: Needs a large model; text-davinci needed a demonstration of how to generate exemplars. Table rows hard to align after extraction.
agent_relevance: Analogy as a model-generated step works, but modestly. Self-written examples can be wrong; the schema should verify them by execution.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: selecting and composing reasoning modules
finding: Closest published match to a heuristic menu. The model picks from 39 atomic reasoning modules, adapts them to the task, and writes a reasoning structure used for every instance of the task. Large gains on non-math BBH and T4D, small on MATH.
numbers: BBH / T4D / MATH. PaLM 2-L: direct 56/30/45, CoT 60/40/42, plan-and-solve 61/42/49, Self-Discover 67/69/50.5. GPT-4: direct 58/51/70.5, CoT 75/52/71, PS 73/53/70, Self-Discover 81/85/73. Beats CoT on 21 of 25 tasks. MATH gain over baselines 1 to 7 (PaLM 2-L) and 2 to 3 (GPT-4) points on a 200-item subsample.
limits: MATH is only 200 problems; the 2-3 point GPT-4 gain is within sampling noise. 74.7 percent of MATH failures came from computation errors even when the structure was right (87.5 percent of structures correct by expert check).
agent_relevance: A task-level choice from a menu is cheap (3 extra calls) and works on structured reasoning tasks. On math the bottleneck is execution, not strategy choice. Supports checks by code over more strategies.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners (COLM 2025)
finding: Four Polya-like behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) in the starting model predict how much RL training improves it. Qwen-2.5-3B has them and reaches about 60 percent on Countdown; Llama-3.2-3B lacks them and reaches about 30 percent. Priming Llama with traces of the behaviours closes the gap.
numbers: Countdown, identical RL: Qwen about 60 percent, Llama about 30 percent. Priming data written by Claude-3.5-Sonnet. In 200,000 sampled OpenWebMath/FineMath documents these behaviours are rare. Continued pretraining set: 8.3 million tokens.
limits: One task (Countdown), 3B models, RL setting. Authors admit priming data are domain-specific. Not a prompting result.
agent_relevance: Heuristic behaviours matter for what a model can learn, but the effect is on training, not on a prompt menu. The base-model difference is a confounder for any prompt-only comparison.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) ablations: which behaviour, and does the answer need to be right
finding: Backtracking was the key behaviour; during RL, models kept backtracking and verification and dropped backward chaining and subgoal setting. Priming with empty or filler thinking tokens gave no benefit (30 to 35 percent), so extra compute alone does not help. Priming with wrong solutions that still showed the behaviours worked as well as with correct ones.
numbers: Empty chain of thought and length-matched filler: 30 to 35 percent, comparable to unprimed Llama. Incorrect-solution priming: reported as identical performance to correct priming (Fig. 6; no table).
limits: Single task. Identical-performance claim is read from a figure, no confidence intervals in text.
agent_relevance: Supports a split of the four behaviours: verify and backtrack are kept; working backwards and subgoals get pruned under outcome reward on this task. Test each operator on its own, G7.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? (ICLR 2025)
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own tests. Chain of thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning. For MMLU, up to 95 percent of CoT gain comes from questions containing an equals sign. The gain is mostly from executing symbolic steps, and a symbolic solver beats it.
numbers: As much as 95 percent of total CoT gain on MMLU attributed to questions with = in the question or output. Other effect sizes not recorded here.
limits: Covers CoT in general, not Polya-style prompts. I read the abstract, introduction and finding statements only.
agent_relevance: Most published gains for reasoning prompts are on math, and math failures are execution failures. A heuristic menu is unlikely to beat code execution for the same tokens.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Look Before You Leap: problem elaboration prompting (PEP)
finding: Have the model restate and elaborate the problem before reasoning (Polya: understand the problem). Gains are largest with GPT-3.5, small or negative on small open models.
numbers: Abstract: +9.93 percent on GSM8K greedy and +8.80 percent with self-consistency (GPT-3.5). Table 3, zero-shot CoT vs PEP, four-set average: Llama2-7B-chat +0.33; Llama2-13B +0.68; Mistral-7B -1.04. GPT-3.5 CoT k=1 vs PEP average +0.48; L2M k=1 +0.65 (rows as extracted).
limits: Headline +9.93 is for one model on one set. Table rows were hard to align after extraction.
agent_relevance: The restate step is a measured, cheap analogue of the Polya understand phase; gain is model-dependent and can be negative. Compare with b07 where restating gave no human benefit.

source: Schorcht, Muller and Buchholtz (2026) No one-size-fits-all: prompt techniques and LLMs for mathematics educational quality (ZDM)
finding: Four LLMs (Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1), six problems, four prompt styles including retrieval of Polya-style heuristics (RAG). Content quality was driven by model and task, not prompt. RAG with the heuristic text was cited in 99 percent of answers but gave no significant gain in content quality; persona prompting improved process and teaching quality most.
numbers: 2880 solutions, human-coded, logistic regression. Algebra vs number tasks OR 21.61. CoT and RAG nearly doubled odds of high process quality vs zero-shot; Persona about sevenfold. Persona raised pedagogical quality odds by 80 percent; RAG positive but not significant.
limits: Measures educational quality of explanations, not answer accuracy. Six tasks, number and algebra only, older models.
agent_relevance: Injecting Polya text into the context changed the form of the answer (it cites the source) but not correctness. Matches Schoenfeld: knowing the heuristic is not control.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve: prompt sensitivity
finding: Authors list prompt sensitivity as a limitation: the GPT-3 models are sensitive to wording, so prompts need careful design. Table 5 compares several trigger sentences on GSM8K and SVAMP.
numbers: Baseline trigger: GSM8K 56.4, SVAMP 69.9. Program-style trigger: 57.0 and 70.8. Not every Table 5 row recorded.
limits: Only part of Table 5 recorded.
agent_relevance: A single heuristic-prompt win on one wording is weak evidence. Any menu test needs several paraphrases and a held-out set.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) fine-grained strategy studies (Heller and Hungate 1985, Silver 1979, 1981)
finding: Studies at fine grain found learnable, usable strategies. Silver showed exploiting related problems is more complex than it looks. Heller and Hungate's five recommendations: make tacit processes explicit, get students talking, guided practice, learn component procedures well, stress both understanding and specific procedures.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary description; underlying studies not opened.
agent_relevance: Operators should be written at the sub-variant level with an explicit procedure and a worked example, not as one-word labels.

source: Newell, quoted in Schoenfeld (1992): Polya revered and Polya ignored
finding: In AI, Polya was seen as wise but too informal to build on: no general rules, only ad hoc examples (Hunt 1975, Minsky 1961). Schoenfeld argues the 1980s turned the evidence in Polya's favour once strategies were specified in detail.
numbers: none
quote: Polya revered, because he is recognized in AI as the person who put heuristic back on the map
limits: Opinion piece quoted in a review.
agent_relevance: Same gap a prompt menu faces: a label is not an operator. Specify trigger, steps, and success check.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting: failure analysis on GSM8K
finding: Nearly every GSM8K problem that least-to-most fails on can be solved with a hand-written decomposition. The bottleneck is choosing the decomposition, which is the planning decision Polya describes.
numbers: Overall GSM8K 60.97 to 62.39 in the text; Table 11 shows the CoT baseline as 60.87.
limits: Internal inconsistency in the paper between 60.97 and 60.87 for the CoT baseline.
agent_relevance: Planning is the weak link, so an independent check on the plan (not the model grading itself) matters. Fits G2 and G3.

source: Bruun (2013) survey of 70 teachers on which strategies they teach
finding: Interviews with 70 grade 2-5 teachers from 42 schools. None taught all the strategies recommended by NCTM. Draw a picture and identify key information were the most taught strategies.
numbers: 70 teachers, 42 schools, one US region.
limits: Self-report, interview study, no student outcomes.
agent_relevance: Which heuristics get taught in practice is driven by ease, not by evidence of effect. Do not copy a curriculum list as an effect ranking.

source: Trinchero and Sala (2016) boundary condition: transfer needs taught heuristics and shared structure
finding: Authors review the chess-to-maths transfer literature, which is mostly negative (Chi 1978: chess players memory did not extend to digits; others on planning and perception). Their own positive result needed heuristics taught explicitly, not mere practice, and tasks sharing structure with chess.
numbers: School-teacher group (no heuristics) d 0.20 vs control 0.13; chess-instructor group d 0.50.
limits: Single study; confounded as in b08.
agent_relevance: Transfer of a heuristic needs shared structure plus explicit teaching. In a prompt, include the cue for when it applies, not only the name.

source: Bruun (2013) on Hembree: step-by-step procedure instructions did worse
finding: Per Hembree, students told to adhere to step-by-step procedures performed lower than students using flexible approaches. Rereading or restating the problem gave no benefit.
numbers: Hembree 1992 pooled 487 reports; effect size values not in this source.
quote: No benefits were found to result from rereading or restating the problem or trying to find solutions purely by trial and error.
limits: Second-hand, Hembree not opened.
agent_relevance: A rigid Polya four-step template in a prompt may hurt on problems it does not fit. Prefer signal-gated operators over a fixed script (G1).

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back: error analysis
finding: On MMLU physics, step-back fixes 20.5 percent of baseline errors and introduces 11.9 percent new ones. Over 90 percent of its remaining errors are not in the abstraction step; reasoning and math errors dominate.
numbers: 20.5 percent fixed, 11.9 percent introduced. Over 90 percent of residual errors in the reasoning stage.
limits: Single benchmark and model for the error count.
agent_relevance: Any heuristic operator both fixes and breaks answers. Net gain depends on the check that decides which answer to keep.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve vs few-shot: where zero-shot plans fall short
finding: PS+ matches but does not clearly beat manually written 8-shot CoT; on MultiArith manual CoT (93.6) and Auto-CoT (95.5) were above PS+ (91.8), and on SVAMP manual CoT (80.3) was above PS+ (75.7).
numbers: text-davinci-003: MultiArith manual 93.6, Auto-CoT 95.5, PS+ 91.8; SVAMP manual 80.3, Auto-CoT 78.1, PS+ 75.7; averages 77.6, 75.9, 76.7.
limits: One model generation.
agent_relevance: A plan prompt substitutes for worked examples only partly. Worked examples of operators remain a lever.
